case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act creates a cause of action against Cuban agencies and instrumentalities that can proceed without satisfying any exception to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082 (including § 6082(c)(1)–(2)), and the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611 (including the baseline grant of immunity and its exceptions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Congress, through Title III, affirmatively authorized U.S. nationals to sue “any person” who traffics in confiscated Cuban property and, in doing so, clearly displaced the FSIA’s default immunity for Cuba’s agencies and instrumentalities (such as CIMEX) at least for Title III trafficking claims. Exxon emphasizes that Congress designed Title III to be an effective compensation-and-deterrence mechanism for Castro-era expropriations, and requiring plaintiffs to separately fit their claims into an FSIA exception would largely nullify that remedy because many trafficking suits would fail on FSIA grounds. The United States (supporting Exxon) highlights § 6082(c)(1) and (c)(2) as textual signals that Congress was specifically addressing jurisdiction over foreign sovereign defendants and thus meant Title III to operate as a standalone jurisdictional path rather than forcing litigants back through FSIA exceptions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: CIMEX and the other respondents argue that the FSIA is the exclusive gateway for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and that Title III does not contain the kind of unmistakably clear statement required to abrogate that immunity or to override the FSIA’s comprehensive framework. In respondents’ view, Title III may create substantive liability and a cause of action, but it does not itself strip sovereign immunity; plaintiffs therefore must plead and prove an FSIA exception (and failing that, the case must be dismissed). They further contend that reading Title III to bypass FSIA would create serious international-law and foreign-relations friction, and that courts should avoid such a construction absent a “super-clear” congressional directive; they also point to structural features (including presidential suspension authority) as inconsistent with an implied, blanket elimination of FSIA protections.
key_precedents: NML Capital, Ltd. v. Republic of Argentina
Kirtz v. (case discussed at argument regarding clear-statement for sovereign immunity; exact full caption not provided in the excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point remains that Title III authorizes suit against “any person” and defines “person” to include foreign “agenc[ies] or instrumentalit[ies],” but that reads most naturally as a substantive-liability choice rather than the unmistakably clear abrogation of sovereign immunity the FSIA requires. Justice Kagan’s harmonization argument is most persuasive under my minimalist approach: we can give Title III full effect while still treating the FSIA as the exclusive jurisdictional gateway, avoiding an implied repeal and adhering to Amerada Hess’s “sole basis” formulation. Justice Barrett’s point that § 6082(c)(1)–(2)’s jurisdiction/service language functions as procedural housekeeping once jurisdiction exists further weakens the claim that Congress silently displaced §§ 1604–1605. The foreign-relations consequences reinforce the clear-statement rule here, so Title III claims may proceed against a foreign state or instrumentality only if an FSIA exception independently supplies jurisdiction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point—that Title III authorizes suit against “any person” and defines “person” to include a foreign “agency or instrumentality”—still reads as a liability rule, not an unmistakably clear abrogation of the FSIA’s immunity-and-exceptions gateway. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, FSIA is a comprehensive, exclusive scheme, and § 6082 nowhere says “notwithstanding the FSIA” or amends §§ 1604–1605; under the rule against implied repeals and our clear-statement cases, that silence is dispositive. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Amerada Hess and Sachs/Simon reinforces that jurisdiction over foreign instrumentalities depends on fitting an FSIA exception, and § 6082(c)(1)–(2) is readily understood as procedural housekeeping once jurisdiction otherwise exists. Under an original public-meaning approach, we enforce the statutes as written: absent an FSIA exception, the court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction even if Title III creates a cause of action.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that Helms–Burton defines “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” but that language is naturally read—as Justice Thomas emphasized—as a substantive liability definition, not an unmistakable jurisdictional abrogation of FSIA immunity. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively frame the right harmonizing move: § 6082(c)(1)–(2)’s jurisdiction/service references can operate as procedural instructions once an FSIA exception supplies jurisdiction, avoiding any implied repeal of § 1604. The cited precedents (Amerada Hess, NML Capital, and as Justice Barrett notes, Sachs/Simon) cut against petitioner because they reinforce the FSIA’s exclusivity and the clear-statement rule in this foreign-relations-sensitive area. Nothing in Title III says “notwithstanding the FSIA” or amends §§ 1604–1607, so under a textualist approach we should not infer a sweeping immunity override with predictable diplomatic consequences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that Title III authorizes suit against “any person” and defines “person” to include foreign agencies or instrumentalities, which suggests Congress contemplated sovereign-linked defendants. But as Justice Kagan explains, that language is naturally read to set substantive liability, while the FSIA still supplies the exclusive jurisdictional gateway absent an unmistakably clear statement to the contrary, and we can harmonize § 6082(c)(1)–(2) as procedural directions once jurisdiction exists. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Sachs and Simon reinforces that the Court continues to treat the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over foreign states and their instrumentalities unless Congress expressly displaces it—something Title III never does (no amendment to §§ 1604–1605, no “notwithstanding FSIA” clause). Given the foreign-relations consequences and our clear-statement rule (Amerada Hess; NML Capital), I am not persuaded that Title III silently abrogates immunity, so plaintiffs must still fit within an FSIA exception.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the abrogation-by-definition move: Title III authorizes suit against “any person” and defines “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” which sounds like Congress contemplated sovereign defendants. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, that goes to who can be liable once in court, not to the distinct, antecedent question whether a foreign instrumentality may be sued at all absent an FSIA exception—Amerada Hess’s “sole basis” formulation and NML Capital’s clear-statement rule cut against treating that definitional choice as an implied jurisdictional override. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Sachs/Simon and her reading of § 6082(c)(1)–(2) as procedural provisions that can operate within FSIA-authorized cases reinforces the harmonization approach and avoids an implied repeal of §§ 1604–1607. On my pragmatic textualist view, the more coherent and workable reading is that Title III supplies a cause of action, while FSIA continues to supply (and limit) jurisdiction unless Congress unmistakably says otherwise.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that Title III defines “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state” and then authorizes suit against “any person,” but that speaks to substantive liability, not the distinct, antecedent question of abrogating sovereign immunity and creating jurisdiction. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, Amerada Hess (and as Barrett notes, Sachs and Simon) treats the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over foreign states absent an unmistakably clear statutory displacement; § 6082 contains no such clear statement (no amendment to §§ 1604–1605 and no “notwithstanding FSIA” clause). The better textual harmonization, consistent with the rule against implied repeals, is that Helms‑Burton supplies a cause of action that can be pursued only when an FSIA exception independently opens the courthouse door. Nothing raised in conference undermines the separation-of-powers and clear-statement principles that counsel leaving any immunity override to Congress to express plainly.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Helms‑Burton defines “person” to include a foreign state’s “agency or instrumentality” and then authorizes suit against “any person,” but that looks like a substantive liability choice, not the unmistakably clear jurisdictional abrogation of FSIA immunity our cases demand. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Amerada Hess and NML Capital is decisive for me: FSIA is the comprehensive, exclusive gateway, and we do not infer an immunity override from general cause-of-action language absent a clear statement. Justice Barrett’s point that § 6082(c)(1)–(2) can be read as procedural directions once jurisdiction exists (rather than a carveout from § 1604) reinforces that the statutes can be harmonized without implied repeal. Given the comity and foreign-relations consequences, institutional legitimacy favors the narrower, textually grounded reading: Title III claims proceed against foreign instrumentalities only when an FSIA exception independently confers jurisdiction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that Title III authorizes suit against “any person” and defines “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” which could be read as inviting suits against sovereign-related defendants. But as Chief Justice Roberts argues, that is naturally a liability definition, and it still does not supply the unmistakably clear statement needed to displace FSIA’s baseline immunity in § 1604 or amend the exclusive exceptions in §§ 1605–1607; Amerada Hess and Sachs counsel against treating general cause-of-action language as an implied jurisdictional override. Justice Kagan’s harmonization point reinforces the textualist path: § 6082(c)(1)–(2) can be read as procedural directions (service/venue/jurisdictional housekeeping) that operate once an FSIA exception independently opens the courthouse door, avoiding an implied repeal with major foreign-relations consequences. No colleague identified precedent that undermines the clear-statement rule here; if anything, Thomas’s reliance on Sachs/Simon confirms that FSIA remains the jurisdictional gateway absent explicit displacement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ best argument remains that Title III’s definition of “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” plus § 6082(c)(1)–(2)’s jurisdiction/service language, signals Congress meant these defendants to be suable; but as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, that reads most naturally as a liability-and-procedure scheme that still operates through the FSIA’s immunity gateway rather than silently displacing it. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Amerada Hess and Sachs/Simon matters for me because those cases treat FSIA exclusivity as a jurisdictional rule: absent an FSIA exception, courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction even if Congress created a substantive cause of action that would otherwise reach the defendant. Pragmatically, and consistent with my fairness-and-workability focus, harmonizing the statutes avoids an implied repeal with major foreign-relations consequences and preserves predictable procedures for both plaintiffs and foreign instrumentalities. I do not see anything in Title III that unmistakably addresses immunity or amends §§ 1604–1605, so the clear-statement requirement is not satisfied.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “comprehensive set of legal standards governing claims of immunity in every civil action against a foreign state,” and § 1604’s baseline immunity is displaced only through an FSIA exception or an unmistakably clear statutory override. Title III of Helms‑Burton, while creating substantive liability against “any person” (22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A)) and defining “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state” (22 U.S.C. § 6023(11)), does not expressly amend the FSIA or clearly state that foreign sovereign immunity is abrogated for these claims, and we do not infer such a repeal by implication absent a direct conflict (Carcieri). The jurisdictional references in § 6082(c)(1)–(2) are at most ambiguous and can be read to operate within the FSIA framework rather than to create a standalone path around it, which better preserves institutional legitimacy and avoids foreign-relations friction absent a super-clear directive. Accordingly, plaintiffs must still satisfy an FSIA exception before proceeding against Cuban agencies and instrumentalities.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA’s text makes immunity the baseline and provides the exclusive set of exceptions through which a court may exercise jurisdiction over a foreign state or its agencies and instrumentalities, see 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604, 1605–1607, 1330(a). Title III’s authorization to sue “any person” who “traffics” in confiscated property, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a), creates substantive liability but does not contain an unmistakably clear statement abrogating FSIA immunity or displacing that comprehensive jurisdictional framework, and §§ 6082(c)(1)–(2) do not expressly override §§ 1604–1605. Our cases describe the FSIA as “the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state,” Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434 (1989), and as a “comprehensive framework,” Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677, 699 (2004), which forecloses inferring an implied repeal from Title III’s general cause-of-action language. Because Exxon has not shown that its Title III claim fits within an FSIA exception, the suit cannot proceed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA provides the “sole basis” for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state or its agencies and instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and a later statute must speak with unmistakable clarity to displace that comprehensive scheme. Republic of Austria v. Altmann and Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess make clear that § 1330 (and the FSIA’s exceptions) displace other jurisdictional pathways, so Title III’s creation of liability against “any person” in 22 U.S.C. § 6082 does not itself eliminate immunity absent an explicit abrogation tied to FSIA. Sections 6082(c)(1)–(2) may address procedural and jurisdictional considerations, but they do not contain the kind of express statement abrogating sovereign immunity or overriding FSIA that this Court has required, and reading them to bypass FSIA would invite serious foreign-relations consequences that Congress did not clearly command. Therefore, plaintiffs must satisfy an FSIA exception to proceed against Cuban agencies or instrumentalities.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and departures from that comprehensive framework require an “unmistakably clear” congressional statement. See Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 439 (1989); Republic of Argentina v. NML Capital, Ltd., 573 U.S. 134, 141 (2014). Title III’s authorization to sue “any person” who “traffics” in confiscated property, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a), and its jurisdiction-related language in § 6082(c)(1)–(2), do not expressly abrogate sovereign immunity or clearly displace FSIA’s immunity-and-exceptions gateway, particularly given the Act’s structure (including presidential suspension authority) and the serious comity and foreign-relations consequences of an implied override. Absent that clear statement, plaintiffs must proceed—if at all—by fitting their claims within an FSIA exception rather than using Title III as a standalone path to hale Cuban instrumentalities into U.S. court.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in federal court,” Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 439 (1989), and Congress must speak with unmistakable clarity to displace that comprehensive framework, see Republic of Argentina v. NML Capital, Ltd., 573 U.S. 134, 140–41 (2014). Title III’s authorization to sue “any person” who “traffics” in confiscated property, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1), reads naturally as creating substantive liability, but it does not expressly address sovereign immunity or amend the FSIA’s exceptions, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1605–1607. The jurisdictional references in § 6082(c)(1)–(2) are too oblique to do the heavy work Exxon assigns them—particularly given the workability and coherence costs of treating Title III as a freestanding end-run around FSIA rather than requiring plaintiffs to identify an applicable FSIA exception. Absent a clear statement that Cuba’s agencies and instrumentalities may be sued notwithstanding the FSIA, I would reconcile the statutes by holding Title III claims may proceed only when an FSIA exception is satisfied.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule of immunity and, as this Court has repeatedly explained, it is the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in our courts.” Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434 (1989); see also NML Capital, Ltd. v. Republic of Argentina, 573 U.S. 134 (2014) (treating the FSIA’s scheme as controlling absent textual authorization). Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act creates a substantive cause of action against “any person,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A), but nothing in § 6082—including § 6082(c)(1)–(2)—contains an unmistakable, express abrogation of foreign sovereign immunity or a clear displacement of the FSIA’s comprehensive jurisdictional gateway for agencies and instrumentalities. Absent that clear statement, and mindful of the rule against implied repeals (Carcieri v. Salazar), the better reading is that Title III operates only where an FSIA exception independently permits suit.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FSIA provides the baseline rule that foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities are immune from suit absent a statutory exception, and it is generally “the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in federal court.” Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 439 (1989). Under NML Capital, the FSIA is a “comprehensive framework,” and Congress may displace it only with an “unmistakably clear” statement; Title III’s creation of a cause of action against “any person,” 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a), does not clearly abrogate FSIA immunity for Cuban agencies and instrumentalities without requiring plaintiffs to satisfy an FSIA exception. The jurisdictional language in § 6082(c)(1)–(2) is at most ambiguous about overriding immunity, and given the strong clear-statement rule in the sovereign-immunity context and the practical foreign-relations consequences, the better institutionalist reading is to harmonize the statutes by requiring an applicable FSIA exception rather than finding an implicit carveout.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the "sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state" in our courts, so absent an applicable FSIA exception a federal court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction. See OBB Personenverkehr AG v. Sachs, 577 U.S. 27, 30 (2015) (quoting Amerada Hess), and Republic of Hungary v. Simon, 604 U.S. 115, 121 (2025). Title III’s authorization to sue "any person" who "traffics" in confiscated property, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a), is naturally read to create substantive liability, but it does not contain an unmistakably clear statement displacing FSIA immunity for Cuban agencies and instrumentalities; §§ 6082(c)(1)–(2) address service and related procedural matters and can be reconciled with continued FSIA gatekeeping rather than treated as an implied carveout. Given the FSIA’s comprehensive framework, see Republic of Argentina v. NML Capital, Ltd., 573 U.S. 134, 141 (2014), I would require plaintiffs to plead and prove an FSIA exception before proceeding against CIMEX.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis” for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and Congress must speak with unmistakable clarity if it intends to displace that comprehensive immunity-and-jurisdiction framework. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp. held that plaintiffs cannot bypass FSIA’s baseline immunity in 28 U.S.C. § 1604 and its enumerated exceptions in §§ 1605–1607 by pointing to another statute, and nothing in Helms‑Burton Title III (including 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2)) contains a sufficiently clear statement that Cuban instrumentalities may be sued notwithstanding FSIA immunity. The better procedural-fairness path is to require plaintiffs to proceed through the FSIA gateway (e.g., commercial-activity or expropriation exceptions) rather than infer an implied displacement with major foreign-relations consequences. Accordingly, Title III may create substantive liability, but it does not itself eliminate FSIA immunity absent a satisfied FSIA exception.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms-Burton Act (LIBERTAD Act) authorizes suits for “trafficking” in expropriated Cuban property against Cuban state agencies/instrumentalities without requiring plaintiffs to separately plead and prove an exception to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms-Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. §§ 6081–6085 (especially § 6082(c)(1)–(2)), in interaction with the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Congress, through Title III, created a cause of action and jurisdictional mechanism designed to allow U.S. nationals to sue not only private “traffickers” but also Cuban government entities that hold and commercially exploit confiscated property; requiring plaintiffs to satisfy a separate FSIA exception would frustrate Title III’s purpose and effectively nullify Congress’s chosen remedy against the primary wrongdoers and their state-owned successors. Petitioner (supported by the United States and business amici) emphasizes Title III’s text and structure—particularly provisions addressing jurisdiction and service on foreign states or their instrumentalities (e.g., § 6082(c)(1)–(2))—as clear-enough evidence that Congress meant to displace the FSIA’s default immunity for this narrow, Cuba-specific category of claims. In the government’s framing, the statutory scheme reflects an intentional tradeoff to promote accountability and compensation for victims of Castro-era expropriations and to advance U.S. foreign-policy interests in democratic transition in Cuba.
case_analysis.respondent_position: CIMEX and other Cuban entities argue that FSIA supplies the exclusive rules for suing foreign states and their instrumentalities in U.S. courts, so Title III claims against Cuban sovereign defendants must fit within an established FSIA immunity exception (e.g., commercial activity, expropriation, etc.). Respondents contend Title III does not contain the kind of unmistakably clear statement required to abrogate sovereign immunity or to displace the FSIA framework; at most, Title III creates liability rules but not a stand-alone immunity override. They stress the strong presumption against implied repeal and the Court’s clear-statement approach in sovereign-immunity cases: if Congress intended to create a Cuba-specific carveout from FSIA, it would have said so expressly. Respondents (supported by foreign-sovereign-immunity and international-law scholar amici) further argue that reading Title III to bypass FSIA would create international-law friction and reciprocity concerns, and that any jurisdictional/service provisions in Title III can be read harmoniously with FSIA rather than as an abrogation.

John Roberts.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest contention is that Title III’s inclusion of “any agency or instrumentality of a foreign state” plus § 6082(c)(1)–(2)’s jurisdiction/service provisions necessarily implies Congress meant to allow suits against sovereign-linked defendants notwithstanding immunity. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Thomas emphasize, our FSIA precedents (Amerada Hess; Verlinden) treat FSIA as the comprehensive, exclusive baseline and require unmistakable clarity—something Title III lacks because it neither amends FSIA nor says foreign-state defendants “shall not be immune” or “notwithstanding” § 1604. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Altmann reinforces the clear-statement principle in sovereign-immunity contexts, making it methodologically improper to infer an immunity abrogation from jurisdictional/service language that can be harmonized as procedural directions once an FSIA exception supplies amenability to suit. A narrow holding that Title III creates a cause of action but does not itself displace FSIA immunity best preserves institutional legitimacy and avoids an implied repeal with significant foreign-relations consequences.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioners’ best argument remains that Title III’s definition of “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” coupled with § 6082(c)(1)–(2)’s jurisdiction and service provisions, implies Congress meant to subject sovereign entities to suit. But implication is not enough where the FSIA’s text makes immunity the default—“shall be immune … except as provided in sections 1605 to 1607”—and nothing in Title III contains the sort of unmistakable language (e.g., “notwithstanding the FSIA” or an amendment to §§ 1605–1607) that would displace that rule. Chief Justice Roberts’s harmonization point is persuasive under a textualist approach: Title III can create a cause of action and procedural directions that operate only once an FSIA exception supplies amenability to suit, avoiding any implied repeal of a comprehensive scheme. The precedents colleagues cite—Amerada Hess and Verlinden (as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes), and Altmann (as Justice Barrett notes)—reinforce that we do not infer immunity abrogation absent clear statutory text, so my vote remains for Respondent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Title III defines “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state” and supplies jurisdiction/service provisions, which on first glance looks like Congress meant these defendants to be sued. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, that is still not the unmistakably clear statement required to displace FSIA’s baseline rule in § 1604 (“shall be immune … except as provided in sections 1605 to 1607”), especially given Amerada Hess and Verlinden’s insistence that FSIA is the comprehensive, exclusive framework. Title III’s § 6082(c)(1)–(2) can operate as procedural directions once (and only once) an FSIA exception supplies amenability to suit, avoiding an implied repeal with serious foreign-relations consequences. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Altmann reinforces the point that when Congress wants to alter immunity rules, it does so explicitly—something Title III conspicuously does not do.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point remains that Title III authorizes suit against “any person,” expressly including an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” and supplies its own jurisdiction/service provisions—text that would be odd if sovereign defendants could never be sued. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, those provisions can sensibly operate once an FSIA exception opens the door, and reading them as a freestanding abrogation would require the kind of implied repeal Amerada Hess and Verlinden caution against in this highly sensitive foreign-relations area. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Altmann reinforces the clear-statement principle here: Congress knows how to say “notwithstanding the FSIA” or to amend §§ 1605–1607 when it intends to strip immunity, and Title III did neither. Pragmatically, requiring plaintiffs to plead an FSIA exception still preserves access to justice in meritorious cases while avoiding unnecessary comity costs and reciprocal exposure for the United States abroad.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Title III’s definition of “person” reaches an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” and § 6082(c)(1)–(2) provides jurisdiction and service mechanics—text that looks like an invitation to sue sovereign-linked entities. But as Chief Justice Roberts persuasively frames it, those provisions can operate coherently as forum/service directions once amenability exists under an FSIA exception, avoiding an implied repeal of § 1604’s default immunity rule. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Altmann and the broader clear-statement principle reinforces that Congress typically speaks expressly when it alters immunity baselines, and Title III never says “notwithstanding FSIA” or amends §§ 1604–1607. On a pragmatic textualist reading that seeks statutory coherence, harmonizing Title III with the FSIA’s exclusive framework (Amerada Hess/Verlinden) is more faithful to the texts than inferring a silent Cuba-specific abrogation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ best textual point remains that Title III authorizes suits against “any person,” expressly including an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” and then supplies its own jurisdiction and service provisions—language that certainly anticipates sovereign-linked defendants. But, as Chief Justice Roberts explains, those provisions can be read harmoniously as procedural instructions that operate only once amenability to suit exists under an FSIA exception, which avoids treating Title III as an implied repeal of § 1604’s default immunity rule (“shall be immune … except as provided in sections 1605 to 1607”). Justice Thomas’s reliance on Amerada Hess and Verlinden reinforces the structural point that FSIA is the exclusive framework for foreign-sovereign immunity and jurisdiction absent unmistakable statutory clarity, and Title III contains no “notwithstanding FSIA” clause, no amendment to §§ 1605–1607, and no express statement that Cuba or its instrumentalities “shall not be immune.” Under clear-statement and anti-implied-repeal principles—especially in foreign-relations-sensitive contexts—I would require plaintiffs to plead and prove an FSIA exception rather than infer an immunity abrogation from Title III’s cause-of-action and procedural text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point remains that Title III defines “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state” and supplies jurisdiction/service provisions, which could be read as an invitation to sue sovereign-linked entities. But as Chief Justice Roberts persuasively frames it, those provisions can be harmonized with the FSIA as procedural directions that operate only after a plaintiff fits within an FSIA exception, avoiding an implied repeal of § 1604’s default immunity rule. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Amerada Hess and Verlinden reinforces that FSIA is the exclusive scheme for immunity and jurisdiction absent unmistakable clarity, and Title III never says “notwithstanding the FSIA,” amends §§ 1605–1607, or otherwise clearly strips immunity. Given the foreign-relations consequences, our clear-statement and anti-implied-repeal principles counsel against inferring an immunity abrogation from Title III’s contemplation of sovereign defendants.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best textual point remains that Title III defines “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state” and then supplies jurisdiction and service provisions in § 6082(c)(1)–(2), which could be read as inviting suits against sovereign-linked entities. But as Justice Kavanaugh and the Chief emphasize, that is not the unmistakably clear statement our precedents require to displace FSIA’s baseline rule in § 1604 that foreign states are immune “except as provided” in §§ 1605–1607; Title III neither amends FSIA nor says “notwithstanding” immunity. Consistent with Amerada Hess/Verlinden’s characterization of FSIA as comprehensive and exclusive, the better harmonizing reading is that Title III creates liability and supplies procedural directions that operate only once an FSIA exception independently opens the courthouse door. No colleague has identified Title III language that squarely overrides immunity rather than merely contemplating sovereign defendants, so my vote remains for the Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Title III’s definition of “person” to include an “agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” coupled with § 6082(c)(1)–(2)’s jurisdiction and service provisions, implies Congress meant sovereign-linked defendants to be haled into U.S. court. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, we can read those provisions as procedural directions that operate only after a plaintiff clears the FSIA threshold, which avoids an implied repeal of § 1604 and preserves the FSIA’s comprehensive framework recognized in Amerada Hess and Verlinden. Justice Barrett’s reference to Altmann reinforces for me that, in the sovereign-immunity context, Congress must speak with unmistakable clarity—language like “notwithstanding the FSIA” or an amendment to §§ 1605–1607—and Title III does neither. Given the comity and reciprocity consequences of treating Title III as a freestanding immunity override, procedural fairness and statutory discipline counsel requiring plaintiffs to plead and prove an FSIA exception.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FSIA provides the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in our courts,” and we have required an unmistakably clear statement before concluding Congress displaced that framework. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434 (1989). Title III’s provisions on jurisdiction and service, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2), can be read as procedural instructions that operate once an FSIA immunity exception is satisfied, rather than as an express abrogation of immunity for Cuban agencies and instrumentalities; absent a clear statement, the presumption against implied repeal counsels harmonizing the statutes. A narrow ruling preserves institutional legitimacy and avoids unnecessary foreign-relations friction by holding that Title III creates a cause of action but does not, on its own, eliminate FSIA immunity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA provides the "sole and exclusive" basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, and its exceptions are exclusive absent an unmistakably clear statutory override. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp. held that 28 U.S.C. § 1330 displaces other jurisdictional grants (including § 1331) in suits against foreign states, and Verlinden likewise treats FSIA as the comprehensive framework for immunity and jurisdiction. Title III’s provisions, including 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2), may create a cause of action and address service, but they do not textually and expressly abrogate immunity or displace FSIA’s immunity rules with the clarity required; thus a plaintiff must plead and prove a specific FSIA exception to proceed. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would require an implied repeal, which we do not presume where the statutes can be harmonized by applying Title III liability only when an FSIA exception to immunity is satisfied.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis” for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state or its instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and Congress must speak with unmistakable clarity to displace that comprehensive scheme. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp. holds that § 1330(a) displaces other jurisdictional grants (including § 1331) for suits against foreign states, and Verlinden reiterates the FSIA’s exclusivity framework absent a clear statutory override. Title III’s provisions in 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2) addressing jurisdiction/service can be read harmoniously with FSIA’s procedures, but they do not expressly abrogate immunity or specify an FSIA exception, and the presumption against implied repeal (Carcieri) counsels against inferring a Cuba-specific carveout from silence. Requiring plaintiffs to plead and prove an FSIA exception preserves the predictable, law-enforcement-and-foreign-relations-sensitive immunity rules Congress enacted in 1976 while still allowing Title III actions where an established exception applies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FSIA supplies the baseline and generally exclusive framework for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its instrumentalities in federal court, and Congress must speak with clear-enough specificity if it means to abrogate that immunity. See Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 439 (1989); Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488–89 (1983). Title III’s jurisdiction and service provisions, including 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2), can be read to facilitate suits when an FSIA exception applies, but they do not unmistakably displace FSIA’s immunity rules for Cuban sovereign defendants. Given the strong presumption against implied repeal and the international-comity stakes, I would require plaintiffs suing Cuban state entities under Title III to plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception rather than treating Title III as a stand-alone immunity override.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSIA establishes the “sole basis” for civil jurisdiction over foreign states and their instrumentalities absent an applicable FSIA exception, and we have required a clear statement before concluding Congress displaced that framework. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp. treated the FSIA as a comprehensive scheme, and nothing in Title III of Helms-Burton unmistakably abrogates immunity or overrides 28 U.S.C. § 1604’s default rule; § 6082(c)(1)–(2)’s jurisdiction/service language can be read to operate only once an FSIA exception supplies jurisdiction rather than to create a freestanding carveout. Given the strong presumption against implied repeal and the workability of harmonizing the statutes, Title III plaintiffs must plead and prove an FSIA exception (e.g., commercial activity or expropriation) to proceed against Cuban state agencies/instrumentalities.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole and exclusive standards” for both jurisdiction and immunity in suits against a foreign state or its instrumentalities, displacing other jurisdictional grants like § 1331. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 435 n.3, 437 (1989); see also Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488, 493 (1983). Title III’s references to jurisdiction and service, including 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2), can be read to operate once an FSIA exception permits the suit; they do not clearly and expressly abrogate foreign sovereign immunity or displace the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme, and we do not lightly infer such a repeal. Absent a clear statement in Title III that Cuba and its instrumentalities are subject to suit notwithstanding the FSIA, plaintiffs must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception, preserving the separation-of-powers judgment Congress made in the FSIA about when U.S. courts may hale foreign sovereigns into court.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FSIA is the “comprehensive” and “exclusive” framework governing when a foreign state or its instrumentalities may be sued in U.S. courts, and § 1604 makes immunity the default “except as provided in sections 1605 to 1607,” a structure this Court has treated as controlling absent a clear statutory override. Title III’s creation of liability for “any person” (including “any agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” 22 U.S.C. § 6023(11)) and its jurisdiction/service provisions in § 6082(c)(1)–(2) show Congress contemplated sovereign defendants, but they do not unmistakably displace FSIA’s immunity rules or add a Cuba-specific immunity exception in the manner our clear-statement and anti-implied-repeal cases require. Reading Helms-Burton to bypass FSIA would work a significant alteration of the immunity baseline with substantial foreign-relations consequences, and under the Court’s institutional practice we should insist Congress speak with greater clarity before concluding it silently revised FSIA’s carefully calibrated scheme. Accordingly, plaintiffs must still plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception for suits against Cuban agencies or instrumentalities.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “comprehensive framework” and “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” in U.S. courts, and Congress must speak with unmistakable clarity if it means to abrogate immunity or displace that framework. Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677, 699 (2004); Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434 (1989). Title III’s provisions in 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2) (addressing jurisdiction and service) can be read to operate within FSIA’s scheme rather than to create a freestanding immunity override, and nothing in Title III expressly amends 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611 or states that Cuban state agencies/instrumentalities “shall not be immune.” Given the presumption against implied repeal and the clear-statement rule in sovereign-immunity cases, plaintiffs bringing Title III claims against sovereign defendants must still plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FSIA supplies the baseline, comprehensive rule that “a foreign state shall be immune … except as provided in sections 1605 to 1607,” 28 U.S.C. § 1604, and this Court has repeatedly treated it as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign sovereign absent an applicable exception. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428 (1989); see also Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677, 699 (2004). Title III’s jurisdiction/service provisions, 22 U.S.C. § 6082(c)(1)–(2), can be read to operate once a defendant is properly amenable to suit under FSIA, but they do not unmistakably abrogate or displace FSIA’s immunity framework, and we generally avoid implied repeals when two statutes can be harmonized. Given the significant comity and reciprocity consequences of bypassing FSIA, procedural fairness and statutory clarity counsel requiring plaintiffs to plead and prove an FSIA exception before proceeding against Cuban state agencies or instrumentalities.
